title: The Real History of Halloween, Told Through a Small Town's Newspapers (Documentary)
alt_titles: Everything You Know About Halloween Is Wrong: The Real History (Documentary)
How a Night of Broken Gates Became Trick-or-Treat: Halloween's Real History
Halloween in Indiana, 1868-2026: What the Old Newspapers Actually Said
description: In 1866, a Philadelphia newspaper described Halloween as the night boys hung dead cats to door-bells. In 1917, an Ontario paper heard gangs shouting "tricks or treats" for the first time. In between, and after, the holiday changed into the one you know.

There was no Celtic god of the dead named Samhain. The church didn't move All Saints' Day to stamp out a pagan festival (the Irish church kept it on April 20). The jack-o'-lantern was a turnip, and the pumpkin version is about 160 years old. Trick-or-treat began as a shakedown. And in nearly 70 years of checking, no child has ever been killed by a stranger's Halloween candy.

This is Halloween as the records show it, stamped MYTH, FACT and NO ONE KNOWS, and what the night looked like in La Porte County, Indiana, from an 1868 shooting over fortune-telling cabbages to today's 5-to-7 p.m. window, read from the newspapers of the towns around us (La Porte's own papers of those years are on microfilm at the county library, not online) and the weather records of the nights themselves.

A La Porte Weather Now documentary (laporteweathernow.com). Narrated by a computer voice. Every painting, print, postcard, photo, map and newspaper page is real, most more than a century old; nothing was drawn by AI. Maps and title cards were drawn for the film.

Samhain and All Saints: Ronald Hutton, The Stations of the Sun (1996); Archaeology magazine (Nov.-Dec. 2016) on the Hill of Ward dig; Vallancey (1786); the Félire Óengusso and the Martyrology of Tallaght

The words and the games: the OED; Merriam-Webster; Montgomerie (1584); Shakespeare; Lisa Morton, Trick or Treat: A History of Halloween (2012); Burns, Halloween (1786); Frank Leslie's Popular Monthly (1895)
Jack and the pumpkin: the Dublin Penny Journal (Jan. 16, 1836); the Kingston Daily News (Nov. 1, 1866); Cindy Ott, Pumpkin (Harper's Weekly, 1867)

America: the Philadelphia Evening Telegraph (Oct. 31, 1866); Godey's Lady's Book (Oct. 1872); the Indiana Historical Bureau's "Devil Cats, Magic Mirrors and Fortune-Telling Cabbage" (Terre Haute and Wabash Express items, 1868-1889); the Dictionary of American Regional English (door-bell night, 1891); History.com (1933)

Northern Indiana: the Lake County Times (Hammond, 1906-1910), South Bend News-Times (1913, 1923) and Indianapolis Journal (1891, 1895) on Chronicling America; the Whiting-Robertsdale Historical Society; the IHB (the Goshen Ghost); Jeff Kenney, "Spooky Spectacle," Towne Post (2023), quoting the Munster Times (1923) and Culver Citizen (1950); the Marion County Historical Society (the 1923 mask vote); Mirror Indy (Irvington); the La Porte County Public Library

Trick-or-treat and after: Barry Popik's word files (1917-1938); UNICEF USA; Joel Best, "Halloween Sadism"; Smithsonian magazine; the National Retail Federation (2026); USDA ERS; the Hesston Steam Museum; WNDU; NOAA/NWS records for South Bend and NWS Northern Indiana and Chicago
